ety.text: From Middle English hegge, from Old English heċġ, from Proto-West Germanic *haggju, from Proto-Germanic *hagjō, from Proto-Indo-European *kagʰyóm (“enclosure”). Cognate with Dutch heg, German Hecke. Doublet of hey (a choreographic figure) and quay. More at haw.
Inherited from Middle English heggen, from the noun (see above).

senses.d: A thicket of bushes or other shrubbery, especially one planted as a fence between two portions of land, or to separate the parts of a garden.
ex: He trims the hedge once a week.

senses.d: A barrier (often consisting of a line of persons or objects) to protect someone or something from harm.
A mound of earth, stone- or turf-faced, often topped with bushes, used as a fence between any two portions of land.
A noncommittal or intentionally ambiguous statement.
Contract or arrangement reducing one's exposure to risk (for example the risk of price movements or interest rate movements).
ex: The asset class acts as a hedge.

senses.d: With indication of a person's upbringing, or professional activities, taking place by the side of the road; being third-rate, poor, shoddy.
ex: He then traced them from place to place, till at last he found two of them drinking together, with a third person, at a hedge-tavern near Aldersgate.
This particular wheelwright is only a hedge carpenter, without even a shop of his own,[…].

senses.d: To enclose with a hedge or hedges.
ex: to hedge a field or garden
Therefore, behold, I will hedge up thy way with thorns, and make a wall, that she shall not find her paths.
Lollius Urbius […] drew another wall […] to hedge out incursions from the north.

senses.d: To offset the risk associated with.

ex: He carefully hedged his statements with weasel words.

senses.d: To construct or repair a hedge.
To reduce one's exposure to risk.
